name: L. K. Advani
role: Indian Deputy Prime Minister (2002-2004) and Home Minister (1998-2004); BJP co-founder and president
summary: Advani is a Hindu nationalist and co-founder of the BJP who led the Ayodhya Ram Janmabhoomi movement and the 1990 Somnath-Ayodhya rath yatra. He describes Hindutva as a cultural way of life, attacks what he calls pseudo-secularism, yet says India's constitution rightly rejects a religious state, and he condemned the 1975 Emergency. As Home Minister he moved the 2002 anti-terror ordinance bill.

clerical-rule.rationale: He described the state he holds up as the ideal as a 'non-theocratic' one with no place for religious extremism or state protection of it (Karachi, 2005).

death-penalty.rationale: As Home Minister he moved the Prevention of Terrorism bill (s8) that became the 2002 Act, whose section 3 makes a terrorist act causing death punishable with death or life imprisonment (s10).

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He condemned the 1975 suspension of fundamental rights and habeas corpus under the Emergency as the eclipse of the rule of law and freedom of expression, and credited the judiciary and the 1977 electorate for the survival of democracy.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In Karachi (2005) he endorsed Jinnah's 1947 address, in which religion has 'nothing to do with the business of the State', as the ideal of a secular, 'non-theocratic' state for India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

religious-nation.rationale: In his Lok Sabha reply of 18 Nov 2002 he said nobody in the Constituent Assembly asked for a Hindu state, that India accepted a constitution of equal rights for Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Parsis, and that Hindutva as he means it is a way of life, not confined to those practising the Hindu faith; Indian Muslims who stayed are 'sons of Mother India'.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: In Karachi (2005) he said the creation of India and Pakistan is an unalterable reality of history that cannot be undone, only some of its follies; asked in his 2014 blog whether an Indo-Pak confederation was still possible, he answered 'Not at all'.

suppress-opposition.rationale: His 2013 blog calls the 1975-77 Emergency a sinister bid to end democracy, recounts the jailing of opposition leaders under MISA (himself included) and the suppression of the press, and in 2015 he said he lacked confidence that civil liberties could not be curtailed again.

surveillance-ok.rationale: As Home Minister he moved the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance bill at the joint sitting of 26 March 2002 (s8), which became the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2002 with a chapter authorising interception of wire, electronic and oral communications in terrorism investigations (s10).

notes: Thin record by the standards of the statement bank: only eight answers rest on text I could open. Searched, with these results: religion and state (Lok Sabha 2002, Karachi 2005, 2020 and 2024 statements on Ayodhya, his 2008 autobiography as reported), civil liberties and the Emergency (2013 blog, 2015 interview), the judiciary (2013 collegium post: he wants the executive's role restored, but no statement matches), elections (fixed tenure, simultaneous elections, mandatory voting: no matching statement), economy (FDI in multi-brand retail opposed in 2012 blogs: no matching statement), nuclear policy, terrorism law (POTO 2002: bill moved by him, Act text read for interception and the death penalty; the Lok Sabha joint-sitting transcript could not be downloaded), Kashmir and Article 370 (blog reports only via snippets), uniform civil code (no statement of his found). His 2002 'pseudo-secularism' remark and Ayodhya movement are not answered because no statement in the bank covers them directly. Failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result.
